subject: blueprintSpitfire
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: Spitfire fighter plane.
Style: cyanotype blueprint.
reasoning:
I'm planning a Spitfire model rendered in cyanotype blueprint style—deep Prussian blue body with white/pale-cyan panel lines, rivets, and grid annotations, treating the propeller as the one jointed part since it's a vehicle rather than a creature.

I'm roughing out realistic Spitfire Mk I proportions—roughly 9.12m length, 11.23m wingspan, 3.86m tail-down height, with a 3.2m diameter three-blade propeller—and positioning the fuselage in a nose-up three-point ground stance with the spinner tip and tail end as reference datum points along the Z-axis.

I'm planning the skeleton structure now: a root body joint plus hinge joints for the propeller, rudder, elevators, and ailerons, with fuselage parts lofted along stations and extrude parts assigned to their respective bones.

Since I can't test API calls live, I'll stick to conservative, well-known calls. For the fuselage loft, I'm working out station placements along the z-axis—tapering from the nose cowling (with spinner base radius ~0.4, cowl width ~0.85) through the wider cockpit section (~0.9 width, ~1.3 height) and back toward the tail.

Writing station coordinates...

I should also add the asymmetric belly radiators under each wing like the real Spitfire, plus a lathe-built spinner cone, cowling ring, and exhaust stacks along the fuselage sides near the nose.

For stance, I'm debating whether to tilt the whole fuselage to the proper 3-point nose-up attitude or keep everything level and just adjust wheel/strut heights -- rotating the root group by the pitch angle around the main wheel contact point seems like the cleaner approach since parts are baked in local space relative to joints.

I'll keep wings level but tilt the fuselage slightly nose-up, with the tail lower than the nose, giving roughly a 5.6° slope. The propeller disc should sit perpendicular to that tilted centerline, so its axis direction points slightly upward and forward rather than straight ahead.

I'm defining a spine line for the fuselage stations, roughly y0(z)=1.72+0.098z, so the top contour rises gently from tail to nose, then building each cross-section as an offset from that curve. For the wings, I'm aiming for the Spitfire's elliptical planform—about 11.23m span, 2.5m root chord, rounded tips, slight dihedral, with the leading edge gently swept and the trailing edge curving forward elliptically, extruding this shape to form the wing volume.

Working through the loft geometry, I'm wrestling with how to give the wing proper airfoil thickness rather than a flat plate—trying to decide whether to loft airfoil cross-sections along the span or sweep a shape along a path, and figuring out which axis ends up representing chord versus thickness given how the orientation frame behaves for a path running along X.

For a sideways-pointing span path, the frame normal lands on world-up and binormal aligns with the chord direction, so I can use an elliptical cross-section with half-chord along that binormal axis and half-thickness along the normal (up) axis, giving roughly 1.25 by 0.15 half-extents, with enough sides on the ellipse to keep it smooth rather than faceted.

Rather than using a shift function to offset the chord center along an ambiguous binormal sign, it's simpler to just build the path directly in absolute coordinates, tracing the chord-centerline with the slight leading/trailing edge sweep baked in, plus a slight upward rise to capture dihedral along the span.

That projection comes out mostly +Y, meaning local X aligns with up and Z becomes the normal — which swaps rx and ry unexpectedly. That's risky, so I should explicitly specify an up vector like [0,1,0] for path sources to fix the starting roll.

So I'll use sweep with that up vector and a radius function returning rx, ry per t, mirroring the same setup for the right wing going toward -X. For the elliptical planform, I'm defining chord as a function of span position using an elliptical falloff, mapping t to span fraction so chord goes to zero at the tip, and setting thickness proportional to chord via a thickness-to-chord ratio around 0.11–0.13 at the root.

I'm leaving camber out for simplicity but adding a leading-edge sweep by shifting the chord centerline back along z as span fraction increases, giving the characteristic elliptical curve where the leading edge sweeps back and trailing edge sweeps forward. Now I'm figuring out where to place the wing root relative to the fuselage, positioning it low with the root near the fuselage bottom and mid-chord roughly aligned with the cockpit area.

Working through the fuselage dimensions at the wing station, I'm computing the root y-position, applying 6° dihedral to get the tip height, and checking that the landing gear legs mounted outboard on the wing have enough length to reach the ground with properly sized wheels, keeping the splayed, outward-retracting Spitfire gear geometry in mind.

Now I'm checking the tail end: figuring out the fuselage bottom height near the tail cone and sizing the tailwheel strut so the aircraft sits correctly in its three-point stance, comparing against real Spitfire proportions to keep things plausible.

Settling on a 0.15 slope gives roughly an 8.5° nose-up angle, placing the tail bottom around 0.70 with the tailwheel strut at 0.55. I'm positioning the fin top near 2.7 and locating the propeller center at the nose.

Working out prop clearance with the tilt, I'm defining a helper function to compute fuselage centerline height along z, keeping wings level while the fuselage axis tilts, and placing the horizontal stabilizer at the tail with a 3.2 span and 1.0 root chord.

I'm thinking through how to build the tailplane as a thin extruded flat plate with beveled edges for rounding, then considering applying a similar sweep-based airfoil approach to the wings, plus adding roundel decals.

For the overall look, I'm leaning toward a blueprint/cyanotype aesthetic—deep Prussian blue tones with crisp white linework and lighter cyan accents, keeping the entire plane rendered in that blue family.

I'm planning concrete annotation details: "SPITFIRE Mk.I" fuselage text, wing dimension arrows, rivet and gridlines. I also want to add thin pale-cyan bulkhead rings swept around the fuselage at intervals to suggest structural section cuts, like a blueprint cross-section detail—maybe eight rings total.

For wing panels I'm planning section-cut lines using plane sweeps perpendicular to the wing's length direction, generating airfoil ring outlines at several spanwise stations on each wing separately.

I should wrap risky surface-dependent decoration calls in try/catch so a degenerate loop doesn't crash the whole build, and now I'm tallying up the part count target, starting with the fuselage.

For the canopy I'm planning a Spitfire-style bubble shape using a scaled sphere geometry for the glassy glazing, tinted light cyan, with thin white frame lines, and lofting the stations from front windscreen to rear to taper the width and height.

Checking the geometry, the canopy center at z=0.5 sits at height 2.4 with span 2.08 to 2.72, rising about half a unit above the fuselage top near 2.2, which looks right for a bubble canopy. I'll add a few thin white frame sweeps around the canopy to suggest the structural ribs.

Since the SDK materials are opaque, I'll just make the canopy a solid light-blue "glass" color with panel lines rather than trying to add transparency or a visible pilot figure—skipping the headrest and pilot head for simplicity. For the nose, I'm setting up a lathed spinner shape with a radius profile that tapers along its length to form the propeller cone.

I'm working out where the spinner should sit relative to the fuselage nose station, nudging it slightly inward so it covers the loft end cap cleanly. Then I'm moving on to the propeller, planning three blades extruded from a blade-shaped outline.

Defining the per-blade coordinate frame...

I'll add a tip color variation, maybe a white band near the tip when the chord coordinate exceeds a threshold, giving a painted tip look. For rigging, I need to figure out the right role for the propeller joint since "hinge" doesn't quite fit — "fan" seems closer, parented appropriately at the spinner, with the fuselage established as the required single root joint and other control surfaces using "hinge".

For the prop hub I'll plan a backplate disk with small cylindrical cuffs where each blade root attaches. For the control surfaces, full aileron geometry risks overlapping the single wing sweep, so I'm leaning toward skipping separate aileron extrudes and instead relying on drawn panel lines, while still giving the tail proper separate parts — a fixed stabilizer plate plus a hinged elevator plate, and a fixed fin plus a hinged rudder plate with their own bones.

Now I'm working out the fin's side-view planform in local coordinates, with forward being +Z and up being +Y, figuring out the swept leading edge, base chord, and height above the fuselage so I can place the fin's origin point correctly at the tail.

Still plotting fin coordinates...

Still placing rudder coordinates...

Working out the tailplane geometry, I'll split it into a fixed stabilizer polygon and separate left/right elevator outlines hinged behind it, defining coordinates for each with x as spanwise and y as the forward-back axis.

Checking the tail geometry, I realize the elevator trailing edge would extend past the fuselage end near the rudder, so I'm shifting the stabilizer position forward to around z=-3.6, which keeps the elevator TE near -4.7 and the leading edge around -3.12, roughly matching the fuselage width there.

Now I'm setting up the elevator thickness and joint hinges for left/right sides, with the left side assigned to the positive X direction. Moving on to wing details, I'm placing the Spitfire's distinctive underwing radiators — the round oil cooler on the left and the square radiator on the right — as boxes positioned roughly at x=±1.8 near the trailing section of the wing.

Writing wing geometry...

Matching the Spitfire profile more closely, I'm setting the wing bottom nearly flush with the fuselage bottom, then working out the main gear leg position and length from the wing geometry at a given span point. For the wing tip, I'm calculating its vertical position using the dihedral angle and planning a curved leading edge via sampled points along a chord path for a smooth catmull spline.

Now I'm defining the wing's chord taper using an elliptical radius function so it narrows smoothly toward the tip, rounding off the very end to avoid an abrupt point, with a 12-sided ring for the cross-section.

The wing's leading edge at the fuselage junction is hidden inside, so the elliptical airfoil shape works fine there without needing a flattened bottom profile. I also want to add the eight machine guns protruding from the leading edges—four per wing, spaced along the span as small barrel cylinders poking forward.

Still writing gun placement...

Now thinking about nav lights at wingtips as small glowing spheres, then working through landing gear geometry -- legs running from the wing mount down to the axles, trying to pin down the actual wheel track width for proper splay.

Designing wheel and tire geometry...

Still working out tire and hub geometry... I'm also placing the tail wheel with its own small tire radius and strut connecting to the fuselage bottom near the tail, positioning it slightly trailing behind.

Now I'm computing the main wheel axle position and the leg geometry, checking where it intersects the wing's lower surface so the strut attaches cleanly inside the wing thickness before extending down to the axle. I'm also considering whether to add a small gear door fairing beside the leg, though I may skip that detail for simplicity.

Still placing the door shape relative to the leg and wheel, checking that it sits slightly outside the splayed leg without clipping into the wheel's position.

I'll keep the door but simplify it with a thin panel and a short connecting rod attaching it to the leg rather than making it a bulky separate part. Now I'm shifting to the exhaust stacks, planning six small spiked stubs per side along the cowl near the fuselage half.

For placing them, I'm computing hit points on the fuselage surface at set elevations and azimuths around a center point for each row, then sticking small boxes there with a null-check guard in case a surface hit fails. Next I'm thinking through the cowling blisters over the cylinder heads, considering small half-sphere or box bumps on the upper hood.

Now I'm planning the roundel decals—concentric white/blue circles as an outlined texture, applied flat on the upper wing surface accounting for dihedral tilt, plus a mirrored version on the fuselage sides facing outward.

I'm also figuring out nose text decals like "SPITFIRE" and a squadron code, considering how the text orientation needs to mirror depending on which fuselage side the viewer sees, since the plane faces forward and left/right sides read differently.

I'm uncertain whether mirroring would make the text look wrong on one side, so to stay safe I'll just place the text on a single side rather than risk a backwards decal. Since the convention is that dir points toward the viewer and the drawing appears unmirrored to someone looking against dir, I can trust the decal to render correctly as drawn.

For the blueprint-style paint, I'm defining panel grid lines and rivet dots that follow surface normals, with simple top-down shading to give the flat blueprint look some sense of form. I'm also calculating texel density for an 11m wingspan aircraft with roughly 150m² of painted surface, settling on a paint resolution where panel lines come out around 1.2cm wide — fine enough to read as rivet detail without being too thin to render.

Each surface type gets its own distinct palette and line treatment: fuselage uses deep navy with ring and stringer grid lines, wings a slightly lighter blue, cowling darker still, canopy glass gets cyan tones with diagonal highlight stripes, and bare metal areas use pale ink-white lines.

I'm also planning smaller detail touches: a radio aerial mast behind the cockpit with a thin white wire running to the fin tip, counting up total parts from bulkheads and wing ribs, and considering whether to add a dorsal fairing or skip extra cockpit details to keep things manageable.

Rather than annotation overlays, I'm now working out the geometry for highlighting the leading and trailing edges of the wings, figuring out which clock angle along the wing tube corresponds to the leading edge based on the direction each wing extends and how "up" and "right" map relative to the fuselage axis.

Adding cowl ring and spinner details...

Working through the station spacing now, I'm computing chord and leading-edge offset at each u-value (0, .2, .4, .55, .7, .8, .9) to build the rib stations, and setting up a dihedral function that raises y linearly with span position, then sweeping the cross-section ribs along this curved path with a fixed up-vector, mirroring for the left wing by negating x.

Writing the wing geometry function...

Checking that the tail fin base and wing root align reasonably with the fuselage contours—the wing bottom sits just slightly below the fuselage bottom at its root, which should merge smoothly enough.
